passage: Experiments on memory consistently find that spacing study sessions apart in time produces better long-term retention than packing the same amount of study into one block—an effect known as the spacing effect. Researchers attribute it to the extra effort of retrieving partly forgotten material when a session resumes after a delay. Because that effortful retrieval is what the massed schedule omits, it follows that a student who crowds an entire term's material into a single night before an exam, with no spaced review along the way, ______
question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: is likely to retain less of the material over the long term than a student who spread the same total study time across the term.
will end up retaining the material over the long term better than a student who chose instead to spread the same total study time evenly across the whole term.
must have spent more total hours studying than a student who relied on spaced review throughout the term.
will be unable to recall any of the material at all when the exam is given the following morning.

explanation: The correct answer is A. The premises are that spaced study produces better long-term retention and that the benefit comes from the effortful retrieval a massed schedule leaves out. A student who crams in one night, with no spacing, omits exactly that retrieval, so the licensed conclusion is reduced long-term retention relative to a spaced schedule of the same total time. Choice B reverses the effect. Choice C makes an unsupported claim about total hours. Choice D overstates the result, predicting total failure to recall, which the passage gives no basis for.
